_comment: Steps shared by open arterial operations (ruptured AAA repair, femoral embolectomy, and future bypass and trauma repairs). Authored once, referenced by many. Procedure-only steps stay in each procedure's steps_local.

step.vasc.vessel-control.title: Proximal and distal control before opening the artery
step.vasc.vessel-control.why: An artery opened without control bleeds at arterial pressure into a field you can no longer see. Control first turns a haemorrhage into a planned arteriotomy.
how: Expose the artery above and below the planned arteriotomy, in healthy tissue away from haematoma or disease where possible.
Pass slings or tapes around each vessel, including the important branches, and identify where each clamp will go before applying any.
Handle the artery by its adventitia or slings, never with forceps on the intima-bearing wall.
State aloud to the anaesthetist when a clamp is going on and when it is coming off.
structuresAtRisk: Accompanying veins, which tear easily during circumferential dissection
Small side branches avulsed by traction on slings
pitfalls: Clamping a heavily calcified segment, which cracks the plaque and causes a dissection.
Dissecting circumferentially around a vessel when a clamp applied from the front would do.

step.vasc.heparin.title: Systemic heparin before clamping
step.vasc.heparin.why: Static blood beyond a clamp clots within minutes. Heparin before clamping prevents distal thrombosis that would undo the repair.
how: Agree the heparin dose with the anaesthetist per local protocol, and give it a few minutes before the clamps go on.
Record the time and dose; check clotting (for example ACT) during long clamp times if the unit uses it.
In active haemorrhage, such as a ruptured aneurysm or trauma, the dose may be reduced or omitted: decide this explicitly and say so.
pitfalls: Clamping before the heparin has circulated.
Forgetting that the patient is heparinised when assessing bleeding at closure.

step.vasc.flush-backbleed.title: Flushing and back-bleeding before the final sutures
step.vasc.flush-backbleed.why: Clot, air and debris left in the lumen go straight to the distal bed when flow is restored. Forward flushing and back-bleeding clear them while you still have control.
how: Before tying the last suture, release the distal clamp briefly to back-bleed, then the proximal clamp to forward-flush.
Irrigate the lumen with heparinised saline and remove any loose thrombus or intimal flaps.
Assess the strength of back-bleeding: weak or absent back-bleeding suggests residual distal thrombus.
pitfalls: Skipping the flush to save a minute at the end of a long operation.
Accepting poor back-bleeding without imaging or further catheter passes.

step.vasc.restore-flow.title: Restoring flow with the anaesthetist warned
step.vasc.restore-flow.why: Declamping releases cold, acidic, potassium-rich blood into the circulation and drops the pressure suddenly. Warned and staged, it is uneventful; unannounced, it can arrest the patient.
how: Tell the anaesthetist before releasing each clamp so that volume and vasopressors are ready.
Release slowly, one limb or one clamp at a time, and be ready to reapply if the pressure falls sharply.
Check the suture lines for bleeding as pressure returns, and repair with fine sutures while still able to clamp.
pitfalls: Releasing both iliac clamps together after a long clamp time.
Chasing suture line bleeding with more sutures before giving heparin reversal, warmth and clotting factors a chance.

step.vasc.perfusion-check.title: Confirming distal perfusion before leaving theatre
step.vasc.perfusion-check.why: A technically perfect anastomosis with a thrombosed or embolised distal bed is a failed operation. The time to find it is while the patient is still on the table.
how: Examine both feet (or hands) under the drapes: colour, capillary refill, palpable pulses, and handheld Doppler signals.
Perform completion angiography or duplex when the result is in doubt, or routinely after embolectomy.
Compare with the pre-operative state and the other limb, and document what you found.
pitfalls: Draping the feet out of view, so that distal ischaemia is found in recovery.
Assuming a poor foot is vasospasm and closing.

step.vasc.vein-mapping.title: Duplex vein assessment and marking
step.vasc.vein-mapping.why: Vein operations succeed or fail on the vein. A conduit that is too small, sclerosed or absent, or a reflux pattern that was assumed rather than shown, is found far more cheaply on the scan than through an incision.
how: Review the duplex report yourself: diameter, depth, continuity, previous thrombosis, and the course of the vein along its length.
Mark the vein on the skin with the patient in the position used for the scan (standing or reverse Trendelenburg for leg veins), the evening before or in the anaesthetic room.
For a venous reflux operation, confirm which segment refluxes and where the junction lies; for a conduit, confirm the length you need and identify a back-up vein.
Repeat the scan on the table with a sterile probe cover when the marking is uncertain.
structuresAtRisk: The vein itself, from failed or repeated cannulation
Adjacent artery mistaken for the vein
pitfalls: Operating on an old scan when the vein has since thrombosed or been used.
Marking with the patient supine, when the vein collapses and the mark drifts.
No back-up conduit identified before the first incision.

step.vasc.vein-harvest.title: Harvesting and preparing a vein conduit
step.vasc.vein-harvest.why: The long-term patency of a vein graft is largely set during harvest. Stretching, crushing, drying, over-distending or leaving a branch untied injures the endothelium and starts the intimal hyperplasia that later blocks the graft.
how: Expose the vein through continuous or skip incisions directly over the marked course, so that the skin flaps are not undermined.
Handle the vein by its adventitia or the stumps of its branches only. Ligate or clip each tributary a short distance from the vein wall, neither flush nor long.
Divide the vein after ligating its ends; mark one surface along its length with a skin marker so that it is not twisted when tunnelled or laid on the heart.
Distend gently with cold heparinised blood or solution through a cannula at low pressure to find leaks, and repair them with fine sutures. Keep the vein moist.
For a reversed graft, label the ends clearly so that the valves face the right way.
structuresAtRisk: Skin flaps over the harvest incision
Lymphatics in the groin and medial thigh
pitfalls: High-pressure distension with a syringe, which tears the intima.
A tie so close to the vein wall that it narrows the lumen, or a branch stump so long that it fills with thrombus.
Losing track of orientation, so that a reversed vein is implanted the wrong way or with a twist.

step.vasc.end-to-side-anastomosis.title: End-to-side anastomosis
step.vasc.end-to-side-anastomosis.why: Most early graft and fistula failures are technical and sit at an anastomosis: a narrowed heel or toe, a lifted intimal flap, a purse-stringed suture line or a twisted conduit. Each is preventable with a deliberate sequence.
how: Make a clean longitudinal arteriotomy in the softest available segment, and cut the end of the conduit obliquely (spatulated) so that its opening matches the arteriotomy.

Start at the heel, using a parachute technique where it helps visibility, and keep equal, small bites with the needle passed from inside to outside on the diseased side so that plaque is pinned rather than lifted.
Take particular care at the toe, where narrowing is most common; place the toe sutures under direct vision, with a probe or dilator in the lumen if needed.
Keep the suture under even tension without purse-stringing, check the lie of the conduit for twist and kinking before the last bites, then flush before tying.
pitfalls: Picking up the back wall in a toe suture.
An arteriotomy too long or too short for the conduit, which narrows the outflow or kinks the hood.
Pulling the continuous suture tight in one go and purse-stringing the anastomosis.

step.vasc.heparin-reversal.title: Deciding on, and giving, heparin reversal
step.vasc.heparin-reversal.why: Protamine reduces wound and mediastinal bleeding, but it can cause severe hypotension, pulmonary hypertension or anaphylaxis, and given at the wrong moment it clots the repair or the bypass circuit. The decision must be explicit and shared with the anaesthetist.
how: Decide with the anaesthetist whether to reverse, the dose per local protocol, and the timing, once flow is restored and the repair is satisfactory.
In cardiac surgery give protamine only after separation from bypass and venous decannulation, and tell the perfusionist so that the pump suckers are switched off before it starts.
Give it slowly while watching the pressure; ask about previous protamine, protamine-containing insulin, or fish allergy beforehand.
Confirm the effect with a clotting test (for example ACT) where the unit uses one, and reassess the operative field afterwards.
structuresAtRisk: Fresh anastomoses and endarterectomised surfaces, which may thrombose if over-reversed
pitfalls: Protamine running while the cardiotomy suckers are still returning blood to the circuit.
Rapid bolus injection causing profound hypotension.
Not stating in the note whether heparin was reversed, leaving the ward unable to interpret bleeding.

step.vasc.groin-closure.title: Layered closure of a groin incision
step.vasc.groin-closure.why: The groin is the commonest site of vascular wound complications: lymph leak, seroma, infection and breakdown over a graft or a vein stump. Closure that obliterates dead space and seals lymphatics reduces all of them.
how: Ligate or seal divided lymphatic tissue rather than leaving it to leak; avoid wide undermining.
Close the deep fascia and subcutaneous tissue in two or more layers so that no cavity remains over the vessels or graft.
Close the skin with a technique that keeps the wound edges everted and away from the groin crease moisture, and apply an occlusive dressing.
structuresAtRisk: Femoral vessels and any graft beneath the closure
pitfalls: A single-layer skin closure over a dead space that fills with lymph.
Deep sutures that catch the graft or the femoral vein.
